Model-Based Reinforcement Learning with Double Oracle Efficiency in Policy Optimization and Offline Estimation

Haichen Hu huhc@mit.edu Affiliation: Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Cambridge, MA 02139, USA    Jian Qian jianqian@hku.hk Affiliation: Department of AI and Data Science Affiliation: The University of Hong Kong Affiliation: Pokfulam Road, Hong Kong    David Simchi-Levi dslevi@mit.edu Affiliation: Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Cambridge, MA 02139, USA
Abstract

Reinforcement learning (RL) in large environments often suffers from severe computational bottlenecks, as conventional regret minimization algorithms require repeated, costly calls to planning and statistical estimation oracles. While recent advances have explored offline oracle-efficient algorithms, their computational complexity typically scales with the cardinality of the state and action spaces, rendering them intractable for large-scale or continuous environments. In this paper, we address this fundamental limitation by studying offline oracle-efficient episodic RL through the lens of log-barrier and log-determinant regularization. Specifically, for tabular Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), we propose a novel algorithm that achieves the optimal O~​(T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T}) regret bound while requiring only O⁡(H​log⁡log​T)O(H\log\log T) calls to both the offline statistical estimation and planning oracles when TT is known and O⁡(H​log⁡T)O(H\log T) calls when TT is unknown. Crucially, this oracle complexity is entirely independent of the size of the state and action spaces. This strict independence drastically reduces the planning oracle complexity, representing a substantial improvement over existing offline oracle-efficient algorithms (Qian et al., 2024). Furthermore, we demonstrate the versatility of our framework by generalizing the algorithm to linear MDPs featuring infinite state spaces and arbitrary action spaces. We prove that this generalized approach successfully attains meaningful sub-linear regret. Consequently, our work yields the first doubly oracle-efficient (i.e., efficient with respect to both statistical estimation and policy optimization) regret minimization algorithm capable of solving MDPs with infinite state and action spaces, significantly expanding the boundaries of computationally tractable RL.

keywords
reinforcement learning, log-barrier, log-determinant, trusted occupancy measure, offline estimation oracle, policy optimization oracle.

1 Introduction

In recent years, Reinforcement Learning (RL), mathematically grounded in the framework of Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), has emerged as a cornerstone of modern machine learning and artificial intelligence. The paradigm of learning optimal sequential decision-making through environmental interaction has yielded remarkable empirical successes across a diverse array of complex, real-world applications. These range from continuous control in robotics (Kober et al., 2013) and autonomous transportation (Kiran et al., 2021), to classical operations research domains such as inventory control and supply chain management (Balseiro et al., 2019; Kastius and Schlosser, 2022). Furthermore, RL has recently played a pivotal role in aligning Large Language Models (LLMs) with human intent via Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) (Ouyang et al., 2022; Dai et al., 2023a), underscoring its broad applicability and transformative impact.

With these broad applications, deploying RL in unknown environments fundamentally requires agents to efficiently navigate the exploration-exploitation trade-off. In the online reinforcement learning setting, an agent must sequentially estimate the underlying environment while actively optimize the executed policies to minimize the cumulative regret against an optimal benchmark. There have been extensive studies on regret minimization algorithms in various MDP models. For tabular MDPs, we have model-based regret minimization (Auer et al., 2008; Azar et al., 2017) and model-free algorithms (Zhang et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2018). For more complex MDPs models, such as linear MDPs, we also have many regret minimization algorithms based on function approximation (Jin et al., 2020b; Dai et al., 2023b; Kim et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2020).

To tackle the intertwined challenges of statistical efficiency and computational complexity under function approximation, a ubiquitous paradigm in the theoretical RL literature is to decouple the two via an oracle-based framework (Foster et al., 2021; Chen et al., 2025). Generally, algorithms proceed by sequentially estimating the unknown environment or value functions using existing data, often invoking a statistical estimation procedure. The agent then feeds this optimistic, estimated model into a policy optimization oracle or planning oracle to compute the next execution policy (Xie et al., 2023; Agarwal et al., 2019).

Within this framework, most existing theoretical regret-minimization algorithms require O⁡(T)O(T) calls to sequential estimation oracles and policy optimization oracles. Such frequent oracle calls can incur substantial computational costs and time overhead, making these algorithms impractical in many real-world applications. Moreover, reinforcement learning typically relies on online estimation oracles to handle adaptively collected data. In contrast to well-studied offline estimation oracles, where the data are collected i.i.d. (Rakhlin, 2022; Vershynin, 2018), online estimation oracles are currently available only for rather limited function classes (Hazan and Koren, 2016). Their construction remains unclear for many complex model classes, such as deep neural networks.

These limitations underscore the need to develop reinforcement learning algorithms that are highly efficient with respect to both policy optimization and offline estimation oracles. To improve policy optimization efficiency, several regret minimization algorithms have been proposed to achieve low switching costs, thereby reducing the computational burden of planning (Bai et al., 2019; Qiao et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021; Qiao et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2021). However, these approaches suffer from several crucial drawbacks. First, they rely on online estimation oracles to update the underlying model. Second, their policy optimization oracle complexity scales with the size of the state and action spaces. Beyond these shared limitations, individual methods exhibit specific weaknesses. For instance, Qiao et al. (2022) is computationally inefficient as it requires enumerating the entire policy version space, while Wang et al. (2021) yields a regret bound that scales exponentially with the feature dimension. Furthermore, although certain algorithms successfully reduce the frequency of actual policy switches, they still necessitate model estimation and policy optimization at every single round (Gao et al., 2021), which is fundamentally not oracle-efficient.

From the perspective of offline oracle efficiency, Simchi-Levi and Xu (2021) pioneered an efficient algorithm for contextual bandits requiring O⁡(log⁡log⁡T)O(\log\log T) offline regression oracle calls with known TT under finite action spaces, which is then generalized to functional regression (Hu et al., 2025a) and general action spaces (Qin and Zhang, 2026). Xu and Zeevi (2020); Levy et al. (2024); Hu et al. (2025b); Levy et al. (2026) introduced UCB-style algorithms to address regret minimization in contextual bandits and tabular contextual MDPs. However, these approaches demand O⁡(T)O(T) oracle calls and are not truly oracle-efficient. Most notably, Qian et al. (2024) proposed the first regret minimization algorithm for tabular MDPs that achieves remarkable efficiency, requiring only O⁡(H​log⁡log​T)O(H\log\log T) offline density estimation oracle calls and O⁡(H​S​A​log⁡log​T)O(HSA\log\log T) policy optimization oracle calls during online interactions.

Nevertheless, all existing algorithms for reinforcement learning suffer from two primary limitations. First, the number of policy optimization (or planning) oracle calls is either O⁡(T)O(T) or scales with the cardinality of the state and action spaces. This dependence becomes computationally prohibitive in environments with large state and action spaces. Therefore, none of them achieves both policy-optimization oracle efficiency and offline estimation oracle efficiency simultaneously. Second, the current literature on offline estimation oracle-efficient regret minimization in reinforcement learning is strictly confined to tabular MDPs (Qian et al., 2024). Consequently, it remains an open question whether offline oracle-efficient algorithms can be developed to achieve sub-linear regret in more complex MDP models. These two limitations naturally motivate the following questions:

Can we design a regret minimization algorithm that is efficient with respect to both offline estimation and planning oracles, with oracle call times entirely independent of the state and action space dimensions?

Furthermore, can we develop offline oracle-efficient regret minimization algorithms for more complex environments beyond tabular MDPs?

Our Contributions.

In this paper, we address both challenges. First, for tabular MDPs with finite state and action spaces, we develop an algorithm that achieves the optimal O~​(T)\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{T}) regret bound while requiring only O⁡(H​log⁡log​T)O(H\log\log T) calls to both the offline estimation oracle and the policy optimization oracle. Notably, in contrast to Qian et al. (2024); Qiao et al. (2023), our oracle-call complexity is entirely independent of the dimensions of the state and action spaces. Thus, our algorithm enjoys a double oracle-efficiency property with respect to both the offline estimation oracle and the policy optimization oracle. Second, we introduce the first offline-oracle-efficient algorithm that achieves meaningful sublinear regret for linear MDPs with infinite state spaces and arbitrary action spaces while maintaining the same minimal O⁡(H​log⁡log​T)O(H\log\log T) oracle-call complexity.

Paper Structure.

The remainder of this paper is organized into two main parts, focusing on tabular MDPs and linear MDPs, respectively. Section 3 introduces the problem setup for tabular MDPs. In Section 4, we present our regret minimization algorithm for the tabular setting, followed by its statistical regret guarantees and a proof sketch in Section 5. We then transition to linear MDPs with infinite state and action spaces in Section 6, where we formalize the model setup. Section 7 details our dual-oracle-efficient regret minimization algorithm for linear MDPs. Finally, Section 8 establishes the corresponding theoretical guarantees.

2 Related Works

Oracle-based reinforcement learning.

Foster and Rakhlin (2020) studies contextual bandits with access to online regression oracles. Later, this framework is generalized to reinforcement learning by Foster et al. (2021) with the E2D algorithm. However, the algorithm requires O⁡(T)O(T) calls to an online density estimation oracle. Compared to our algorithm, these algorithms need significantly more calls to an oracle that is harder to implement for many model classes. Later, Simchi-Levi and Xu (2021) reduces regret minimization in contextual bandits to offline regression with O⁡(log⁡log⁡T)O(\log\log T) oracle calls under known TT. Moreover, Xu and Zeevi (2020) studied regret minimization for contextual bandits using the “Optimism in Face of a Context” principle with O⁡(T)O(T) calls to an offline oracle. Later, Levy and Mansour (2023) generalize the idea to tabular MDPs with reachability assumptions. More recently, Levy et al. (2024); Levy et al. (2026) further removed the reachability assumption and obtained O⁡(T)O(\sqrt{T}) regret rate with O⁡(T)O(T) offline estimation oracle calls. For offline oracle efficiency, Qian et al. (2024) proposed the first offline oracle-efficient regret minimization algorithm for tabular MDPs with only O⁡(H​log⁡log​T)O(H\log\log T) oracle calls but O⁡(H​S​A​log⁡log​T)O(HSA\log\log T) planning oracle calls.

By comparison, we achieve the optimal regret bound in the tabular MDP setting using only O⁡(H​log⁡T)O(H\log T) or O⁡(H​log⁡log​T)O(H\log\log T) calls to both the offline estimation and planning oracles—a complexity that is completely independent of the state and action space dimensions. This strict independence represents a substantial improvement over existing algorithms. Furthermore, it enables our method to be the first doubly oracle-efficient algorithm that attains meaningful sub-linear regret in MDPs with infinite state and action spaces. See Table 1 for a summary.

Learning with log-barrier regularization.

At a technical level, our algorithm is rooted in log-barrier and log-determinant regularization. While log-barrier penalties have been widely utilized in online and reinforcement learning to guide exploration or ensure safety (Foster et al., 2016; Hazan, 2016; Zheng et al., 2019; Wei and Luo, 2018; Cesani et al., 2026; Usmanova et al., 2024; Ni and Kamgarpour, 2025; Zhang et al., 2024), and have been adapted for adversarial settings (Dai et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2023; Zimmert and Lattimore, 2022), their integration into offline oracle-efficient RL remains underexplored. Foster et al. (2020) demonstrated the equivalence between log-barrier regularization and inverse gap weighting, subsequently generalizing it via the log-determinant for infinite spaces. Motivated by these insights, our method introduces a novel integration of log-barrier regularization with a trusted occupancy measure adapted from Qian et al. (2024). This carefully designed combination not only significantly reduces the number of planning oracle calls but also seamlessly extends to MDPs with infinite state and action spaces. Consequently, we successfully achieve offline oracle-efficient RL in these complex environments, directly resolving the setting where Qian et al. (2024) falls short.

We adopt standard Bachmann-Landau notation O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) and O~​(⋅)\widetilde{O}(\cdot), where A=O⁡(B)A=O(B) means A≤BA\leq B up to a constant factor, and A=O~​(B)A=\widetilde{O}(B) means A≤BA\leq B up to logarithmic factors. For a finite set 𝒳\mathcal{X}, we use |𝒳||\mathcal{X}| to denote its cardinality. For a countable space 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, ∫𝒴\int_{\mathcal{Y}} denotes the integral over 𝒴\mathcal{Y} with respect to the counting measure. For any set ℬ\mathcal{B}, we let Δ⁡(ℬ)\Delta(\mathcal{B}) denote the set of all probability distributions supported on ℬ\mathcal{B}.

3 Tabular MDP Model Setup

We consider an episodic online reinforcement learning setting with a finite trajectory horizon number HH. A tabular Markovian decision process is defined by the tuple (M,𝒮,𝒜,s1)(M,{\mathcal{S}},\mathcal{A},s^{1}), where 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} is a finite state space with |𝒮|=S|{\mathcal{S}}|=S and 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a finite action space with |𝒜|=A|\mathcal{A}|=A. A model MM is represented by {Ph,rh}h=1H\left\{P^{h},r^{h}\right\}_{h=1}^{H}, where PhP^{h} denotes the transition kernel and rhr^{h} denotes the expected reward function. More specifically, the transition kernel satisfies ℙh​(sh+1=s′∣sh=s,ah=a)=Ph​(s′∣s,a)\mathbb{P}^{h}(s_{h+1}=s^{\prime}\mid s_{h}=s,a_{h}=a)=P^{h}(s^{\prime}\mid s,a), and the expected reward at step hh is given by rh​(s,a)r^{h}(s,a) when the agent takes action aa in state ss.

In Markovian decision processes, however, the decision maker does not know the true underlying model. Instead, he must learn the model through sequential interaction with the environment. In episodic reinforcement learning, the decision made by the DM throughout every trajectory is called a policy, which is denoted by π\pi. Specifically, any policy π\pi can be modeled as a mapping sequence (π1,⋯,πH)(\pi^{1},\cdots,\pi^{H}), where πh:𝒮→Δ⁡(𝒜)\pi^{h}:{\mathcal{S}}\rightarrow\Delta(\mathcal{A}) is a mapping from the state space 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} to the probability simplex of the action space 𝒜\mathcal{A}. We use ΠR​N​S\Pi_{RNS} to denote the set of all randomized, non-stationary policies.

Let TT denote the total number of trajectories and M∗M_{*} denote the true model, i.e., M∗={P∗h,r∗h}h∈[H]M_{*}=\{P^{h}_{*},r^{h}_{*}\}_{h\in[H]}. The interactive protocol proceeds in TT rounds. In each round tt, the tt-th trajectory is generated by the following process:

  • •

    The decision maker starts with a fixed known initial state st1=s1∈𝒮s_{t}^{1}=s^{1}\in{\mathcal{S}}.

  • •

    The decision maker chooses policy πt=(πt1,⋯,πtH)\pi_{t}=(\pi_{t}^{1},\cdots,\pi_{t}^{H}) to apply.

  • •

    For step h=1:Hh=1:H:

    • –

      The DM samples action atha_{t}^{h} according to the randomized policy πth(⋅|sth)∈Δ(𝒜)\pi_{t}^{h}(\cdot|s_{t}^{h})\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}).

    • –

      The DM moves to the next state sth+1s_{t}^{h+1} according to the Markov transition kernel

      sth+1∼P∗h(⋅|sth,ath),s_{t}^{h+1}\sim P_{*}^{h}(\cdot|s_{t}^{h},a_{t}^{h}),

      and receives stochastic reward Rth​(sth,ath)=r∗h​(sth,ath)+ξtR_{t}^{h}(s_{t}^{h},a_{t}^{h})=r_{*}^{h}(s_{t}^{h},a_{t}^{h})+\xi_{t}.

Here, ξt\xi_{t} is zero-mean random noise that is independent of the DM’s decisions. Without loss of generality, throughout the paper, we assume that the total reward gathered in every trajectory ∑h=1HRh\sum_{h=1}^{H}R^{h} is bounded in [0,1][0,1].

In this paper, we consider the model-based reinforcement learning under the well-specified case. Specifically, we assume that we have a model class ℳ\mathcal{M} from which M∗M_{*} can be learned, which is called the realizability assumption in reinforcement learning. {assumption} We have a model class ℳ\mathcal{M} such that the true underlying model M∗∈ℳM_{*}\in\mathcal{M}.

Dynamic Programming.

We now provide some basic background about dynamic programming (Sutton et al., 1998). Given any model MM, policy π\pi, state ss and action aa, we define the QQ function QMh​(s,a,π)Q_{M}^{h}(s,a;\pi) at layer hh and the value function VMh​(s,π)V_{M}^{h}(s;\pi) at layer hh as

QMh(s,a;π)=∑j=hH𝔼M,π[Rj|sh=s,ah=a],andVMh(s;π)=𝔼a∼πh(⋅|s)[QhM(s,a;π)].Q_{M}^{h}(s,a;\pi)=\sum_{j=h}^{H}\mathbb{E}^{M,\pi}[R^{j}|s^{h}=s,a^{h}=a],\ \text{and}\ V^{h}_{M}(s;\pi)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi^{h}(\cdot|s)}[Q_{h}^{M}(s,a;\pi)].

Then, we have the Bellman equation

QMh​(s,a,π)=rMh​(s,a)+∫s′∈𝒮PMh​(s′|s,a)​VMh+1​(s′,π).Q_{M}^{h}(s,a;\pi)=r^{h}_{M}(s,a)+\int_{s^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{S}}}P_{M}^{h}(s^{\prime}|s,a)V_{M}^{h+1}(s^{\prime};\pi).

We denote π∗\pi_{*} as the optimal policy of the true model M∗M_{*} and abbreviate its QQ function and value function as QM∗h​(⋅,⋅)Q_{M_{*}}^{h}(\cdot,\cdot) and V∗h​(⋅)V_{*}^{h}(\cdot). When h=1h=1, we further simplify the notation by representing V∗1​(s1)V_{*}^{1}(s^{1}) as V∗1V_{*}^{1} and VM∗1​(s1,π)V_{M_{*}}^{1}(s^{1},\pi) as V∗1​(π)V_{*}^{1}(\pi).

For any model M={Ph,rh}h∈[H]M=\{P^{h},r^{h}\}_{h\in[H]} and any policy π\pi, we let M⁡(π)M(\pi) denote the distribution of the trajectory (s1,a1,r1,…,sH,aH,rH)(s^{1},a^{1},r^{1},\ldots,s^{H},a^{H},r^{H}) induced when the learner follows policy π\pi and the environment evolves according to model MM. Correspondingly, we use ℙM,π\mathbb{P}^{M,\pi} and 𝔼M,π\mathbb{E}^{M,\pi} to denote the probability and expectation under M⁡(π)M(\pi). We also write M⁡(k)M(k) for the kk-th layer of the model, namely M⁡(k)={Pk,rk}M(k)=\left\{P^{k},r^{k}\right\} for k=1,2,…,Hk=1,2,\ldots,H. Therefore, estimating the model MM is equivalent to estimating each layer M⁡(k)M(k) for all k∈[H]k\in[H].

Offline Density Estimation Oracles.

In the Tabular MDP setting, we consider offline density estimation oracles associated with the model class ℳ\mathcal{M}, denoted by Algoff\texttt{Alg}_{\texttt{off}}. Specifically, given any two distributions ℙ\mathbb{P} and ℚ\mathbb{Q} and some base measure μ\mu, the Hellinger divergence between them is defined as

DH2​(ℙ,ℚ):=∫(d​ℙd​μ−d​ℚd​μ)2​𝑑μ.D_{\mathrm{H}}^{2}(\mathbb{P},\mathbb{Q}):=\int\left(\sqrt{\frac{d\mathbb{P}}{d\mu}}-\sqrt{\frac{d\mathbb{Q}}{d\mu}}\right)^{2}d\mu.

In the Tabular MDP model estimation in this paper, we are interested in the following offline regression statistical guarantee on the Hellinger divergence.

Given nn training trajectories (πi,si1,ai1,Ri1,⋯,siH,aiH,RiH)(\pi_{i},s_{i}^{1},a_{i}^{1},R_{i}^{1},\cdots,s_{i}^{H},a_{i}^{H},R_{i}^{H}), i=1,2,⋯,ni=1,2,\cdots,n such that {πi}i=1n\left\{\pi_{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{n} are drawn i.i.d. from pp, and (si1,ai1,Ri1,⋯,siH,aiH,RiH)(s_{i}^{1},a_{i}^{1},R_{i}^{1},\cdots,s_{i}^{H},a_{i}^{H},R_{i}^{H}) is the trajectory sampled according to M∗​(πi)M_{*}(\pi_{i}). The offline density estimation oracle 𝙰𝚕𝚐𝚘𝚏𝚏\mathtt{Alg}_{\mathtt{off}} returns an estimator M^\widehat{M}. For any δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, we have

𝔼π∼p​[DH2​(M^​(π),M∗​(π))]≤ℰℳδ​(n).\mathbb{E}_{\pi\sim p}[D_{\mathrm{H}}^{2}(\widehat{M}(\pi),M_{*}(\pi))]\leq\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta}(n).

When ℳ\mathcal{M} is finite and the density estimation oracle Algoff\texttt{Alg}_{\texttt{off}} is maximal likelihood estimation, the offline density estimation oracle Algoff\texttt{Alg}_{\texttt{off}} yields the guarantee ℰℳδ​(n)≲log⁡(|ℳ|/δ)n\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta}(n)\lesssim\frac{\log(|\mathcal{M}|/\delta)}{n} by Lemma 23. For more general model classes, we bound ℰℳδ​(n)\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta}(n) via Dudley’s entropy integral. In this paper, we make the following assumption on the offline density estimation oracle Algoff\texttt{Alg}_{\texttt{off}}. {assumption} ℰℳδ​(n)\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta}(n) is decreasing in nn and δ\delta. Specifically, for any n1<n2n_{1}<n_{2}, we have ℰℳδ​(n1)>ℰℳδ​(n2)\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta}(n_{1})>\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta}(n_{2}). For any δ1<δ2\delta_{1}<\delta_{2}, we have ℰℳδ1​(n)>ℰℳδ2​(n)\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta_{1}}(n)>\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta_{2}}(n). This assumption is natural. As the number of training samples increases, the estimation error is expected to decrease; on the other hand, a stronger confidence requirement typically results in a weaker guarantee.

Policy Optimization Oracles.

In reinforcement learning, the statistical estimation oracles only help us estimate the model, but they do not provide concrete guidance about which policies should be executed. This is usually done by the policy optimization oracles. Usually, given a reinforcement learning model MM, a policy optimization oracle solves the following optimization problem:

π^∈argmaxπ∈ΠR​N​SJ⁡(π,M),\widehat{\pi}\in\mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}_{\pi\in\Pi_{RNS}}J(\pi;M),

where JJ is an objective function that is parametrized by the model MM. For instance, in reinforcement learning, with an estimated model M^=(P^h,R^h)h=1H\widehat{M}=(\widehat{P}^{h},\widehat{R}^{h})_{h=1}^{H}, a UCB-type regret minimization algorithm uses the policy optimization oracle to maximize the estimated cumulative reward ∑h=1HR^h\sum_{h=1}^{H}\widehat{R}^{h} plus an exploration bonus term bhb_{h} (Auer et al., 2008; Ayoub et al., 2020), i.e.

J⁡(π,M^)=𝔼M^,π​[∑h=1H(R^h​(sh,ah)+bh​(sh,ah))].J(\pi,\widehat{M})=\mathbb{E}^{\widehat{M},\pi}[\sum_{h=1}^{H}(\widehat{R}^{h}(s_{h},a_{h})+b_{h}(s_{h},a_{h}))].

Meanwhile, in pure-exploration reinforcement learning (Jin et al., 2020a), the objective is, broadly speaking, to encourage the agent to visit every state-action pair at every step. This motivates the use of entropy-based objectives in policy optimization oracles, as in maximum-entropy exploration methods (Hazan et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2021). Accordingly, at each step hh, we adopt the Rényi entropy as the policy optimization objective

Jh​(π,M^)=11−α​log⁡(∑s,a(dM^h​(s,a,π))α),J_{h}(\pi,\widehat{M})=\frac{1}{1-\alpha}\log(\sum_{s,a}(d^{h}_{\widehat{M}}(s,a;\pi))^{\alpha}),

where dM^hd^{h}_{\widehat{M}} is the occupancy measure at step hh under the estimated model M^\widehat{M}.

The performance measure of the decision maker is denoted by the total expected regret. Specifically, the regret of policy π\pi is defined as

reg⁡(π):=V∗1−V∗1​(π).\mathrm{reg}(\pi):=V_{*}^{1}-V_{*}^{1}(\pi).

Correspondingly, the total expected regret of the decision maker is defined by

Reg⁡(T):=∑t=1T𝔼t​[reg⁡(πt)],\mathrm{Reg}(T):=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{t}[\mathrm{reg}(\pi_{t})],

where 𝔼t[⋅]=𝔼[⋅|ℋt]\mathbb{E}_{t}[\cdot]=\mathbb{E}[\cdot|\mathcal{H}_{t}] is the expectation conditioned on the history up to round tt.

4 Double Oracle Efficient Reinforcement Learning: Tabular MDP

In this section, we present our algorithm design about reinforcement learning with double efficiency in tabular MDPs. Specifically, we will first provide an overview and show that our algorithm enjoys double oracle efficiency in the offline statistical density estimation oracle and in the policy optimization oracle in Subsection 4.1. Then, we provide the construction details and the ideas behind the algorithm in Subsection 4.2.

4.1 Algorithm Design

The algorithm proceeds in the following way. For the whole interaction process with TT rounds, we divide it into NN epochs. An epoch schedule is defined as a finite sequence: 0=τ0<τ1<⋯<τN=TH0=\tau_{0}<\tau_{1}<\cdots<\tau_{N}=\frac{T}{H}. The concrete values of τ1,τ2,⋯,τN\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\cdots,\tau_{N} will be specified later. For any round number tt, we use m⁡(t)m(t) to denote the epoch it belongs to. For any epoch mm, it lasts H⁡(τm−τm−1)H(\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1}) rounds. Furthermore, each epoch is divided evenly into HH segments, and every segment contains τm−τm−1\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1} rounds. In the hh-th segment in epoch mm, the learner applies a deterministic policy π^mh\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m}, which is determined at the beginning of this segment. Then, the decision maker executes policy πt=π^mh\pi_{t}=\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m} in this trajectory. Moreover, after collecting the data from all the trajectories in the hh-th segment of the mm-th epoch, {πt}∪{stj,atj,Rtj}j=1H\left\{\pi_{t}\right\}\cup\{s_{t}^{j},a_{t}^{j},R_{t}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{H} for τm−1​H+(τm−τm−1)​(h−1)+1≤t≤τm−1​H+(τm−τm−1)​h\tau_{m-1}H+(\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1})(h-1)+1\leq t\leq\tau_{m-1}H+(\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1})h. We call our offline regression oracle Algoff\texttt{Alg}_{\texttt{off}} with this trajectory data as the input and obtain an estimated model M^mh={(P^m,hj,r^m,hj)j=1H}\widehat{M}^{h}_{m}=\left\{(\widehat{P}^{j}_{m,h},\widehat{r}^{j}_{m,h})_{j=1}^{H}\right\}. For this estimated model, we will only be interested in the hh-th layer of this output, i.e., the estimated Markovian transition kernel P^m,hh\widehat{P}^{h}_{m,h} from step hh to step h+1h+1 and the estimated reward function r^m,hh\widehat{r}^{h}_{m,h} at step hh. Then, we aggregate our estimated models into one approximated model and feed this model into the next epoch m+1m+1.

Specifically, for the aggregation process, we first know that at any fixed epoch mm, there are HH estimated models

M^mh={(P^m,hj,r^m,hj)j=1H},h=1,2,⋯,H.\widehat{M}_{m}^{h}=\left\{(\widehat{P}^{j}_{m,h},\widehat{r}^{j}_{m,h})_{j=1}^{H}\right\},\ h=1,2,\cdots,H.

For each specific model M^mh\widehat{M}_{m}^{h}, we only use its output at layer hh. More specifically, we extract its estimated transition kernel P^m,hh\widehat{P}^{h}_{m,h} and its estimated reward function r^m,hh\widehat{r}^{h}_{m,h} at step hh. Repeating this operation for every layer h∈[H]h\in[H] and then combining the corresponding outputs across all HH layers, we obtain an aggregated estimated model produced by epoch mm, denoted by M^mo​u​t\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}, given by

M^mo​u​t={(P^m,hh,r^m,hh)h=1H}.\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}=\left\{(\widehat{P}^{h}_{m,h},\widehat{r}^{h}_{m,h})_{h=1}^{H}\right\}.

We now introduce some additional notation used in both the algorithm and the analysis. Given the estimated models {M^mo​u​t}m=1N\left\{\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}\right\}_{m=1}^{N}, we define V^mh​(s,π):=VM^mo​u​th​(s,π)\widehat{V}_{m}^{h}(s;\pi):=V_{\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}}^{h}(s;\pi) and Q^mh​(s,a,π):=QM^mo​u​th​(s,a,π)\widehat{Q}_{m}^{h}(s,a;\pi):=Q_{\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}}^{h}(s,a;\pi) for each h∈[H]h\in[H]. Correspondingly, let π^m\widehat{\pi}_{m} denote an optimal policy in the estimated environment M^mo​u​t\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}. We further define the pseudo-regret of a policy π\pi as reg^m​(π):=V^m1​(π^m)−V^m1​(π)\widehat{\mathrm{reg}}_{m}(\pi):=\widehat{V}_{m}^{1}(\widehat{\pi}_{m})-\widehat{V}_{m}^{1}(\pi). Moreover, for each step hh, we denote the transition kernel and reward function of the model M^mo​u​t\widehat{M}_{m}^{out} by P^mh(⋅∣s,a)\widehat{P}_{m}^{h}(\cdot\mid s,a) and r^mh​(s,a)\widehat{r}_{m}^{h}(s,a), respectively.

To better illustrate the algorithm structure, we have the following Figure 1 to show how the algorithm proceeds within every epoch.

Finally, with the preceding ingredients in place, we present the pseudocode of our algorithm, DOERL, in Algorithm 1.

4.2 Per-Epoch Detailed Construction: Tabular MDP

The main technical nontrivial construction in our paper is a novel truncated log-barrier regularization. We first define the so-called trusted probability transition set and trusted occupancy measure, which is first studied by Qian et al. (2024). The idea of the trusted transition set is to eliminate the state-action transition pairs that occur too scarce.

We first introduce the concept of occupancy measure in reinforcement learning.

Definition 2.

For any model MM, at any step hh, under any policy π\pi, we use dMh​(s,a,π)d_{M}^{h}(s,a;\pi) to denote the probability of visiting state action pair (s,a)(s,a) under policy π\pi under model MM, i.e.,

dMh​(s,a,π)=ℙM,π​(sh=s,ah=a).d_{M}^{h}(s,a;\pi)=\mathbb{P}^{M,\pi}(s_{h}=s,a_{h}=a).
Definition 3.

For any mm, hh, we iteratively define the trusted occupancy measures d~mh​(s,π)\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s;\pi), d~mh​(s,a,π)\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi) and the set of trusted transition set 𝒯~mh\widetilde{{\mathcal{T}}}^{h}_{m} at layer hh as the following:

d~m1​(s,π)=𝕀⁡(s=s1),d~m1​(s,a,π)=𝕀⁡(s=s1)​π1​(a|s),\widetilde{d}^{1}_{m}(s;\pi)=\mathbb{I}(s=s^{1}),\ \widetilde{d}^{1}_{m}(s,a;\pi)=\mathbb{I}(s=s^{1})\pi^{1}(a|s),
d~mh+1​(s,π)=∫(s,a,s′)∈𝒯~mh+1d~mh​(s,a,π)​P^mh​(s|s′,a′),\widetilde{d}^{h+1}_{m}(s;\pi)=\int_{(s,a,s^{\prime})\in\widetilde{{\mathcal{T}}}^{h+1}_{m}}\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi)\widehat{P}^{h}_{m}(s|s^{\prime},a^{\prime}),
d~mh+1​(s,a,π)=d~mh+1​(s,π)​πh+1​(a|s).\widetilde{d}^{h+1}_{m}(s,a;\pi)=\widetilde{d}^{h+1}_{m}(s;\pi)\pi^{h+1}(a|s).

The set of the trusted transition set 𝒯~mh+1\widetilde{{\mathcal{T}}}^{h+1}_{m} is defined as

𝒯~mh+1:={(s,a,s′)|d~mh​(s,a,π^mh)⋅P^mh​(s′|s,a)≥1ζm},\widetilde{{\mathcal{T}}}^{h+1}_{m}:=\left\{(s,a,s^{\prime})\Big|\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m})\cdot\widehat{P}^{h}_{m}(s^{\prime}|s,a)\geq\frac{1}{\zeta_{m}}\right\},

where ζm\zeta_{m} is a parameter that we can tune. We will specify the choice of ζm\zeta_{m} later.

Our trusted occupancy measure is iteratively well-defined. Specifically, to compute d~mh+1\widetilde{d}^{h+1}_{m}, which is used in the h+1h+1-th segment of epoch mm, we only need access to {𝒯~mj+1,P^mj}j∈[h]\left\{\widetilde{{\mathcal{T}}}^{j+1}_{m},\widehat{P}^{j}_{m}\right\}_{j\in[h]}, which has already been estimated and computed during the first hh segments in epoch mm.

For the true model M∗M_{*}, we define the true observable occupancy measure as

d1​(s,π)=𝕀⁡(s=s1),d1​(s,a,π)=d1​(s,π)​π1​(a|s)d^{1}(s;\pi)=\mathbb{I}(s=s^{1}),d^{1}(s,a;\pi)=d^{1}(s;\pi)\pi^{1}(a|s)
dmh+1​(s,π)=∫(s′,a′,s)∈𝒯~mh+1dmh​(s,a,π)​P∗h​(s|s′,a′).d^{h+1}_{m}(s;\pi)=\int_{(s^{\prime},a^{\prime},s)\in\widetilde{{\mathcal{T}}}^{h+1}_{m}}d^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi)P_{*}^{h}(s|s^{\prime},a^{\prime}).
dmh+1​(s,a,π)=dmh+1​(s,π)​πh+1​(a|s).d^{h+1}_{m}(s,a;\pi)=d^{h+1}_{m}(s;\pi)\pi^{h+1}(a|s).

Recall that after completing all HH segments in epoch mm, we obtain the model M^mo​u​t={(P^m,hh,r^m,jh)h=1H}\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}=\left\{(\widehat{P}^{h}_{m,h},\widehat{r}^{h}_{m,j})_{h=1}^{H}\right\}, which may be viewed as a summary of epoch mm. For this model M^mo​u​t\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}, we define the estimated occupancy measure as

d^mh​(s,π):=𝔼M^mo​u​t,π​[𝕀⁡(sh=s)],d^mh​(s,a,π):=𝔼M^mo​u​t,π​[𝕀⁡(sh=s,ah=a)].\widehat{d}^{h}_{m}(s;\pi):=\mathbb{E}^{\widehat{M}^{out}_{m},\pi}[\mathbb{I}(s^{h}=s)],\ \widehat{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi):=\mathbb{E}^{\widehat{M}^{out}_{m},\pi}[\mathbb{I}(s^{h}=s,a^{h}=a)].

Thus, from the construction, our trusted occupancy measure d~mh\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m} in Definition 3 can be viewed as a layer-wise truncation of d^mh\widehat{d}^{h}_{m}.

Therefore, we can see that the policy optimization oracle and the offline density estimation oracle call times are both N​HNH, where NN is the epoch number. Later in Section 5, we will show that by appropriate epoch scheduling, we have N≍log⁡log⁡TN\asymp\log\log T and our algorithm enjoys a O⁡(H​log⁡log​T)O(H\log\log T) low frequency oracle call property.

Compared with the trusted occupancy measure proposed by Qian et al. (2024), which takes the form {(s,a,s′)|maxπ∈ΠR​N​S⁡{d~mh​(s,a,π)S​A⋅P^mh​(s′|s,a)}≥1ζm}\left\{(s,a,s^{\prime})|\max_{\pi\in\Pi_{RNS}}\left\{\frac{\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi)}{SA}\cdot\widehat{P}^{h}_{m}(s^{\prime}|s,a)\right\}\geq\frac{1}{\zeta_{m}}\right\}, our new construction is significantly more efficient to implement. Specifically, we do not need to optimize over the entire policy space to determine whether a (s,a,s′)(s,a,s^{\prime}) tuple lies in the trusted transition set. Instead, our trusted transition set takes the form {(s,a,s′)|d~mh​(s,a,π^mh)⋅P^mh​(s′|s,a)≥1ζm}\left\{(s,a,s^{\prime})|\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m})\cdot\widehat{P}^{h}_{m}(s^{\prime}|s,a)\geq\frac{1}{\zeta_{m}}\right\}, which is naturally computable from the previously applied policy π^mh\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m}.

The objective function that we optimize at the beginning of segment hh in epoch mm:

V^m−11​(π)+1ηm​∑s,alog⁡(d~mh​(s,a,π)+βm),\widehat{V}^{1}_{m-1}(\pi)+\frac{1}{\eta_{m}}\sum_{s,a}\log(\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi)+\beta_{m}),

can be viewed as the estimated value function with a log-barrier regularization (Foster et al., 2016) weighted by the parameter ηm\eta_{m}. Specifically, the first term in the objective, V^m1​(π)\widehat{V}_{m}^{1}(\pi), captures exploitation since maximizing this value function amounts to maximizing the total expected reward along the trajectory. In contrast, the log-barrier term encourages exploration (Foster et al., 2020): maximizing this quantity is closely related to maximizing the entropy (Zhang et al., 2021), thereby promoting broader exploration of the environment (Dai et al., 2023b; Jin et al., 2023). Therefore, by tuning the weight parameter ηm\eta_{m}, the policy achieves a suitable exploration-exploitation trade-off and thus controls the overall regret.

5 Theoretical Guarantees: Tabular MDP

In this section, we provide our theoretical regret guarantee for Tabular MDPs. We present our results in the following order. In Subsection 5.1, we present the per-epoch theoretical guarantees regarding bounding the value function estimation error via the pseudo-regret. Specifically, we provide several important lemmas that are extremely useful for deriving such guarantee, which is illustrated in the proof sketch of Lemma 7. Later, in Subsection 5.2, we determine the values of the hyper-parameters in Algorithm 1, namely, τm,ζm,βm,ηm\tau_{m},\zeta_{m},\beta_{m},\eta_{m}, m=1,2,⋯m=1,2,\cdots. Finally, we combine the per-epoch guarantees in Subsection 5.1 to prove the main regret guarantee.

5.1 Per-Epoch Theoretical Analysis

In this subsection, we bound the value function estimation error between M∗M_{*} and the estimated model M^mout\widehat{M}_{m}^{\mathrm{out}} using the pseudo-regret evaluated under the previous model, M^m−1out\widehat{M}_{m-1}^{\mathrm{out}}. To establish such results, we need intermediate lemmas that connect the trusted occupancy measure with the estimated occupancy measure and the true observable occupancy measure.

Lemma 4.

For any s,as,a and any policy π′\pi^{\prime}, we have

d~mh​(s,a,π′)≤(d~mh​(s,a,π^mh)+βm)​(S​A+ηm​reg^m−1​(π′)).\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi^{\prime})\leq(\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m})+\beta_{m})(SA+\eta_{m}\widehat{\mathrm{reg}}_{m-1}(\pi^{\prime})).

Lemma 4 implies that the difference of the trusted occupancy measure of any policy π′\pi^{\prime} is upper bounded by that of the selected policy π^mh\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m} up to some other minor terms. Intuitively, as long as we can show that d~mh\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m} is also close to the real estimated occupancy measure, Lemma 5 indicates that our executed policy satisfies some maximum “entropy” exploration guarantee, which is why we can just use a single policy π^mh\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m} to construct the trusted occupancy measure, unlike Qian et al. (2024).

To control the discrepancy between d~mh\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m} and d^mh\widehat{d}^{h}_{m}, we have the following lemma.

Lemma 5.

For any π,h,s,a,m\pi,h,s,a,m, we have

d^mh​(s,a,π)−d~mh​(s,a,π)≤H​S3​A3ζm+ηm​H​S2​A2​reg^m−1​(π)ζm+H​S2​A2​(1+ηm​reg^m−1​(π))​βm.\widehat{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi)-\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi)\leq\frac{HS^{3}A^{3}}{\zeta_{m}}+\frac{\eta_{m}HS^{2}A^{2}\widehat{\mathrm{reg}}_{m-1}(\pi)}{\zeta_{m}}+HS^{2}A^{2}(1+\eta_{m}\widehat{\mathrm{reg}}_{m-1}(\pi))\beta_{m}.

Lemma 5 successfully links the trusted occupancy measure with the estimated occupancy measure. However, in order to bound the value function estimation error, we need to control the difference between d~mh\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m} and the true observable occupancy measure dmhd^{h}_{m}, which is summarized in the following lemma.

5.2 Regret Analysis

In this subsection, we prove the regret guarantee. First, we determine the optimal and valid values of our hyper-parameters. Then, to be concrete, we will explicitly state the result with the finite model class settings where ℰℳδ​(n)≲log⁡(|ℳ|/δ)n\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta}(n)\lesssim\frac{\log(|\mathcal{M}|/\delta)}{n}. Summary.

This concludes our discussion on tabular MDPs with finite state-action spaces. In this setting, we introduced an algorithm that achieves optimal regret with respect to TT while requiring infrequent calls to both the policy optimization and statistical offline density estimation oracles. In the subsequent section, we extend our focus to linear MDPs with infinite state and action spaces. We will present an algorithm that successfully reduces online regret minimization to statistical offline regression. To facilitate this, we introduce a modified trusted occupancy measure and a novel log-determinant regularization technique to guide our policy selection.

6 Linear MDP Model Setup

6.1 Motivation and Technical Difficulty

In tabular MDPs, regret bounds typically scale with the cardinalities of the state and action spaces, which involves “the curse of dimensionality” (Bellman, 1966). In many practical settings, however, the state space may be infinite, and the action space may be highly unstructured. Developing online regret minimization algorithms for such environments, while maintaining dual efficiency with respect to both the offline estimation oracle and the policy optimization oracle, is therefore a highly challenging problem. In this paper, going beyond the tabular setting, we further study linear MDPs and propose the first algorithm that achieves sublinear regret using only low-frequency calls to an offline regression oracle and a policy optimization oracle for linear MDPs with infinite state and action spaces.

Technically, achieving offline-oracle-efficient learning for linear MDPs is substantially more challenging, and the previous approach about defining the trusted occupancy measure no longer applies. At a high level, this difficulty arises because the state and action spaces are now infinite. As a result, unlike in tabular MDPs where the state action pairs are finite, in linear MDPs with infinite state action spaces, we can no longer afford to verify every (s,a,s′)(s,a,s^{\prime}) tuple and establish entrywise guarantees for each individual transition. Instead, we must develop statistical guarantees at an aggregate level by integrating over the newly defined trusted occupancy measures. To address this challenge, we introduce a new notion of trusted transition set and trusted occupancy measure that is capable of handling the infinite-dimensional state and action structure of linear MDPs.

We present our results on double oracle efficient reinforcement learning under the linear MDP setting in the following order. In Subsection 6.2, we provide our linear MDP model setup, some notations and necessary assumptions. Later in Section 7, we introduce our algorithm design and the detailed construction of our new method for linear MDPs. Finally, in Section 8, we provide the theoretical guarantee and regret analysis of our algorithm.

6.2 Linear MDP

A linear Markovian decision process is defined by the tuple (M,𝒮,𝒜,s1)(M,{\mathcal{S}},\mathcal{A},s^{1}), where 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} is the state space, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the action space, and s1∈𝒮s^{1}\in{\mathcal{S}} is a fixed starting state. MM denotes the decision-making model. Specifically, for any model MM, the adaptive decision-making process can be modeled by the following tuple M={ϕh,μh+1,rh}h=1HM=\left\{\phi_{h},\mu^{h+1},r^{h}\right\}_{h=1}^{H}, where ϕh:𝒮×𝒜→ℝd\phi_{h}:{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} is a feature map and μh+1:𝒮→ℝd\mu^{h+1}:{\mathcal{S}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d} is the coefficient vector mapping. d>1d>1 is the feature dimension. In the linear MDP model MM, at step h∈[H]h\in[H] within any trajectory, if a learner applies action ah=aa_{h}=a at state sh=ss_{h}=s, then the transition probability that they will move to sh+1=s′s_{h+1}=s^{\prime} in the next step is characterized by the following Euclidean inner product in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}:

ℙh​(sh+1=s′|sh=s,ah=a)=⟨ϕh​(s,a),μh+1​(s′)⟩.\mathbb{P}^{h}(s_{h+1}=s^{\prime}|s_{h}=s,a_{h}=a)=\left\langle\phi_{h}(s,a),\mu^{h+1}(s^{\prime})\right\rangle.

rh:𝒮×𝒜→ℝ+r^{h}:{\mathcal{S}}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{+} is the expected reward function of model MM, i.e., the DM receives a stochastic reward whose expectation equals rh​(s,a)r^{h}(s,a) if he applies action aa at state ss in step h∈[H]h\in[H] under model MM. In the linear MDP model MM, the expected reward is likewise parameterized linearly in the feature map ϕh\phi_{h}, that is, rh​(s,a)=⟨ϕh​(s,a),θh⟩r^{h}(s,a)=\left\langle\phi_{h}(s,a),\theta^{h}\right\rangle for some unknown coefficient vector θh∈ℝd\theta^{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. In this paper, we use the collections {ϕh,μh+1,rh}h=1H\left\{\phi_{h},\mu^{h+1},r^{h}\right\}_{h=1}^{H} and {ϕh,μh+1,θh}h=1H\left\{\phi_{h},\mu^{h+1},\theta^{h}\right\}_{h=1}^{H} interchangeably to denote the linear MDP model MM. In the linear MDP setting in this paper,we assume that the state space 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} is countably infinite and the action space 𝒜\mathcal{A} is arbitrary.

In linear MDPs, the feature mappings {ϕh}h∈[H]\left\{\phi_{h}\right\}_{h\in[H]} are known to the decision maker, and the coefficient vectors {μ∗h+1​(⋅),θ∗h}h∈[H]\{\mu^{h+1}_{*}(\cdot),\theta_{*}^{h}\}_{h\in[H]} are unknown and need to be estimated. Just as in Section 3, we also assume that we have a model class ℳ\mathcal{M} where M∗M_{*} can be learned from. {assumption} We have a model class ℳ\mathcal{M} such that the true underlying model M∗∈ℳM_{*}\in\mathcal{M}. Apart from realizability, following Mhammedi et al. (2023); Modi et al. (2024). we also need some normalization assumption about the coefficient vector mapping. Specifically, in this paper, we consider the following normalization condition.

Definition 12.

For a linear MDP model M={(ϕh,μh+1,θh)h=1H}M=\left\{(\phi_{h},\mu^{h+1},\theta^{h})_{h=1}^{H}\right\}, we say that MM satisfies the normalization condition if there exists cM<∞c_{M}<\infty such that for any h∈[H]h\in[H],

∫s′∈𝒮‖μh+1​(s′)‖1/2≤cM<∞,‖θh‖2≤1.\int_{s^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{S}}}\|\mu^{h+1}(s^{\prime})\|^{1/2}\leq c_{M}<\infty,\ \|\theta^{h}\|_{2}\leq 1.

Definition 12 is automatically satisfied in tabular MDPs with cMc_{M} set to 11 for all tabular MDPs. With Definition 12, in this section, we assume that the normalization condition is true for all the models in our model class ℳ\mathcal{M}. {assumption} Given the model class ℳ\mathcal{M} in Assumption 6.2, for all h∈[H]h\in[H], the feature map ϕh\phi_{h} satisfies ‖ϕh​(s,a)‖2≤1\|\phi_{h}(s,a)\|_{2}\leq 1 for all s∈𝒮s\in{\mathcal{S}} and all a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}. Moreover, for all M∈ℳM\in\mathcal{M}, MM satisfies the normalization condition in Definition 12, and cℳ=supM∈ℳcM<∞c_{\mathcal{M}}=\sup_{M\in\mathcal{M}}c_{M}<\infty.

Similar to the tabular setting, for any linear MDP M={(ϕh,μh+1,θh)}h∈[H]M=\{(\phi_{h},\mu^{h+1},\theta^{h})\}_{h\in[H]} and policy π\pi, M⁡(π)M(\pi) is the distribution of the trajectory (s1,a1,r1,…,sH,aH,rH)(s^{1},a^{1},r^{1},\ldots,s^{H},a^{H},r^{H}) when the learner follows policy π\pi in model MM. Correspondingly, ℙM,π\mathbb{P}^{M,\pi} and 𝔼M,π\mathbb{E}^{M,\pi} denote the probability and expectation under M⁡(π)M(\pi). We also write M⁡(k)M(k) for the kk-th layer of the model, namely M⁡(k)={ϕk,μk+1,rk}M(k)=\left\{\phi_{k},\mu^{k+1},r^{k}\right\} for k=1,2,…,Hk=1,2,\ldots,H.

Offline Regression Oracles.

For linear MDPs, instead of the Hellinger distance, we consider the L2L^{2} distance between two distributions. Specifically, given any two distributions ℙ\mathbb{P} and ℚ\mathbb{Q} and some base measure μ\mu, the L2L^{2} distance between them is defined as

‖ℙ−ℚ‖L22:=∫|d​ℙd​μ−d​ℚd​μ|2​𝑑μ.\|\mathbb{P}-\mathbb{Q}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}:=\int\lvert\frac{d\mathbb{P}}{d\mu}-\frac{d\mathbb{Q}}{d\mu}\rvert^{2}d\mu.

For linear MDP model estimation, we need the following offline regression statistical guarantee on L2L^{2} distance.

Definition 13.

Given nn training trajectories (πi,si1,ai1,Ri1,⋯,siH,aiH,RiH)(\pi_{i},s_{i}^{1},a_{i}^{1},R_{i}^{1},\cdots,s_{i}^{H},a_{i}^{H},R_{i}^{H}), i=1,2,⋯,ni=1,2,\cdots,n such that {πi}i=1n\left\{\pi_{i}\right\}_{i=1}^{n} are drawn i.i.d. from pp, and (si1,ai1,Ri1,⋯,siH,aiH,RiH)(s_{i}^{1},a_{i}^{1},R_{i}^{1},\cdots,s_{i}^{H},a_{i}^{H},R_{i}^{H}) is the trajectory sampled according to M∗​(πi)M_{*}(\pi_{i}). The offline regression oracle 𝙰𝚕𝚐𝚘𝚏𝚏\mathtt{Alg}_{\mathtt{off}} returns an estimator M^\widehat{M}. For any δ∈(0,1/2)\delta\in(0,1/2), with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, we have

𝔼π∼p​[‖M^​(π)−M∗​(π)‖2]≤ℰℳδ​(n).\mathbb{E}_{\pi\sim p}[\|\widehat{M}(\pi)-M_{*}(\pi)\|^{2}]\leq\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta}(n).

When ℳ\mathcal{M} is finite, and the offline regression oracle Algoff\texttt{Alg}_{\texttt{off}} is the least square estimation, we have that ℰℳδ​(n)≲log⁡(|ℳ|/δ)n\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta}(n)\lesssim\frac{\log(|\mathcal{M}|/\delta)}{n}. Similar to the offline density estimation oracle used in tabular setting, we make the following assumption on the offline regression oracle Algoff\texttt{Alg}_{\texttt{off}}. {assumption} ℰℳδ​(n)\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta}(n) is decreasing in nn and δ\delta. 7 Double Oracle Efficient Reinforcement Learning: Linear MDP

We now present our algorithm design in the following order. First, we will provide an overview of the structure of our algorithm and the pseudo-code in Subsection 7.1. Then, in Subsection 7.2, we present the construction details and ideas of our learning algorithm.

7.1 Algorithm Design

Similar to Algorithm 1, we divide the TT total rounds into NN epochs following the schedule 0=τ0<⋯<τN=TH0=\tau_{0}<\cdots<\tau_{N}=\frac{T}{H}. Each epoch mm is evenly split into HH segments of τm−τm−1\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1} rounds. During the hh-th segment of epoch mm, we execute a fixed deterministic policy π^mh\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m} and collect trajectory data {πt}∪{stj,atj,Rtj}j=1H\left\{\pi_{t}\right\}\cup\{s_{t}^{j},a_{t}^{j},R_{t}^{j}\}_{j=1}^{H}. We input this data into the offline regression oracle Algoff\texttt{Alg}_{\texttt{off}} to obtain the estimated model M^mh={(ϕj,μ^m,hj+1,r^m,hj)j=1H}\widehat{M}^{h}_{m}=\left\{(\phi_{j},\widehat{\mu}^{j+1}_{m,h},\widehat{r}^{j}_{m,h})_{j=1}^{H}\right\}. From this, we extract only the hh-th layer’s transition kernel ⟨ϕh​(⋅,⋅),μ^m,hh+1​(⋅)⟩\left\langle\phi_{h}(\cdot,\cdot),\widehat{\mu}^{h+1}_{m,h}(\cdot)\right\rangle and reward function r^m,hh\widehat{r}^{h}_{m,h}, aggregating these layer-wise estimates into a single approximate model to feed into the next epoch m+1m+1.

For each specific model M^mh\widehat{M}_{m}^{h}, we only use its output at layer hh. Then, similar to the tabular setting, we obtain an aggregated estimated model at the end of epoch mm, denoted by M^mo​u​t\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}, given by

M^mo​u​t={(ϕj,μ^m,jj+1,θ^m,jj)j=1H}.\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}=\left\{(\phi_{j},\widehat{\mu}^{j+1}_{m,j},\widehat{\theta}^{j}_{m,j})_{j=1}^{H}\right\}.

Continuing with standard notations for the estimated model M^mo​u​t\widehat{M}_{m}^{out} in the tabular setting, we define V^mh​(s,π):=VM^mo​u​th​(s,π)\widehat{V}_{m}^{h}(s;\pi):=V_{\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}}^{h}(s;\pi) and Q^mh​(s,a,π):=QM^mo​u​th​(s,a,π)\widehat{Q}_{m}^{h}(s,a;\pi):=Q_{\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}}^{h}(s,a;\pi) for h∈[H]h\in[H]. Let π^m\widehat{\pi}_{m} be the optimal policy under M^mo​u​t\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}, with pseudo-regret reg^m​(π):=V^m1​(π^m)−V^m1​(π)\widehat{\mathrm{reg}}_{m}(\pi):=\widehat{V}^{1}_{m}(\widehat{\pi}_{m})-\widehat{V}^{1}_{m}(\pi). Furthermore, for step hh, we denote the transition kernel ⟨ϕh​(s,a),μ^m,hh+1​(⋅)⟩\left\langle\phi_{h}(s,a),\widehat{\mu}^{h+1}_{m,h}(\cdot)\right\rangle as P^mh(⋅|s,a)\widehat{P}^{h}_{m}(\cdot|s,a) and the reward ⟨ϕh,θ^m,hh⟩\left\langle\phi_{h},\widehat{\theta}^{h}_{m,h}\right\rangle as r^mh​(s,a)\widehat{r}^{h}_{m}(s,a). Finally, we present the pseudo-code in Algorithm 2.

7.2 Per-Epoch Detailed Construction: Linear MDP

The main technical nontrivial construction in our paper is a novel truncated log-determinant regularization. We first define the so-called trusted probability transition set and trusted occupancy measure, which differ from the previous definitions in Section 4.

Definition 14.

For any mm, hh, we iteratively define the trusted occupancy measures d~mh​(s,π)\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s;\pi), d~mh​(s,a,π)\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi) and the set of trusted transition set 𝒯~mh\widetilde{{\mathcal{T}}}^{h}_{m} at layer hh as the following:

d~m1​(s,π)=𝕀⁡(s=s1),d~m1​(s,a,π)=𝕀⁡(s=s1)​π1​(a|s),\widetilde{d}^{1}_{m}(s;\pi)=\mathbb{I}(s=s^{1}),\ \widetilde{d}^{1}_{m}(s,a;\pi)=\mathbb{I}(s=s^{1})\pi^{1}(a|s),
d~mh+1​(s,π)=∫s′,a′d~mh​(s,a,π)​⟨ϕh​(s′,a′),μ^m,hh+1​(s)⟩​𝕀​(s′∈𝒯~mh+1),\widetilde{d}^{h+1}_{m}(s;\pi)=\int_{s^{\prime},a^{\prime}}\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi)\left\langle\phi_{h}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}),\widehat{\mu}^{h+1}_{m,h}(s)\right\rangle\mathbb{I}(s^{\prime}\in\widetilde{{\mathcal{T}}}^{h+1}_{m}),
d~mh+1​(s,a,π)=d~mh+1​(s,π)​πh+1​(a|s).\widetilde{d}^{h+1}_{m}(s,a;\pi)=\widetilde{d}^{h+1}_{m}(s;\pi)\pi^{h+1}(a|s).

The set of the trusted transition set 𝒯~mh+1\widetilde{{\mathcal{T}}}^{h+1}_{m} is defined as

𝒯~mh+1:={s′|∫s,ad~mh​(s,a,π^mh)⋅⟨ϕh​(s,a),μ^m,hh+1​(s′)⟩≥1ζm},\widetilde{{\mathcal{T}}}^{h+1}_{m}:=\left\{s^{\prime}\Big|\int_{s,a}\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m})\cdot\left\langle\phi_{h}(s,a),\widehat{\mu}^{h+1}_{m,h}(s^{\prime})\right\rangle\geq\frac{1}{\zeta_{m}}\right\},

where ζm\zeta_{m} is a parameter that we can tune. We will specify the choice of ζm\zeta_{m} later.

Our trusted occupancy measure is iteratively well-defined. To compute d~mh+1\widetilde{d}^{h+1}_{m}, we only need access to {𝒯~mj,μ^m,jj+1}j∈[h]\left\{\widetilde{{\mathcal{T}}}^{j}_{m},\widehat{\mu}^{j+1}_{m,j}\right\}_{j\in[h]}, which has already been estimated and computed during the first hh segments in epoch mm.

Note that this definition differs significantly from Definition 3. One primary reason for this divergence is the vast state-action space, which precludes us from exhaustively checking every (s,a,s′)(s,a,s^{\prime}) transition as is feasible in tabular MDPs. Furthermore, the selection criterion used in the tabular setting is overly stringent; naively applying the previous definition here could result in the excessive elimination of valid transitions.

For the true model M∗M_{*}, we define the true observable occupancy measure as

d1​(s,π)=𝕀⁡(s=s1),d1​(s,a,π)=d1​(s,π)​π1​(a|s)d^{1}(s;\pi)=\mathbb{I}(s=s^{1}),d^{1}(s,a;\pi)=d^{1}(s;\pi)\pi^{1}(a|s)
dmh+1​(s,π)=∫s′,a′dmh​(s,a,π)​⟨ϕh​(s′,a′),μ^∗h+1​(s)⟩​𝕀​(s′∈𝒯~mh+1).d^{h+1}_{m}(s;\pi)=\int_{s^{\prime},a^{\prime}}d^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi)\left\langle\phi_{h}(s^{\prime},a^{\prime}),\widehat{\mu}^{h+1}_{*}(s)\right\rangle\mathbb{I}(s^{\prime}\in\widetilde{{\mathcal{T}}}^{h+1}_{m}).
dmh+1​(s,a,π)=dmh+1​(s,π)​πh+1​(a|s).d^{h+1}_{m}(s,a;\pi)=d^{h+1}_{m}(s;\pi)\pi^{h+1}(a|s).

Recall that after completing all HH segments in epoch mm, we obtain the model M^mo​u​t={(ϕj,μ^m,jj+1,r^m,jj)j=1H}\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}=\left\{(\phi_{j},\widehat{\mu}^{j+1}_{m,j},\widehat{r}^{j}_{m,j})_{j=1}^{H}\right\}, which may be viewed as a summary of epoch mm. For this model M^mo​u​t\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}, we define the estimated occupancy measure as

d^mh​(s,π):=𝔼M^mo​u​t,π​[𝕀⁡(sh=s)],d^mh​(s,a,π):=𝔼M^mo​u​t,π​[𝕀⁡(sh=s,ah=a)].\widehat{d}^{h}_{m}(s;\pi):=\mathbb{E}^{\widehat{M}^{out}_{m},\pi}[\mathbb{I}(s^{h}=s)],\ \widehat{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi):=\mathbb{E}^{\widehat{M}^{out}_{m},\pi}[\mathbb{I}(s^{h}=s,a^{h}=a)].

Given the trusted occupancy measures, for any policy π\pi, we define the feature covariance matrix, weighted by the trusted occupancy measure, as follows.

K~mh​(π):=∫s,aϕh​(s,a)​ϕh​(s,a)T​d~mh​(s,a,π).\widetilde{K}^{h}_{m}(\pi):=\int_{s,a}\phi_{h}(s,a)\phi_{h}(s,a)^{T}\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi).

Intuitively, we can view d~mh\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m} as a truncation of the estimated occupancy measure d^mh\widehat{d}^{h}_{m} of the K~mh​(π)\widetilde{K}^{h}_{m}(\pi) integrating ϕh​ϕhT\phi_{h}\phi_{h}^{T} over the sub-probability measure d~mh\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}.

With the truncated feature matrix K~mh\widetilde{K}^{h}_{m}, for any policy π\pi, we define the truncated log-determinant regularization term as

Λmh​(π):=1ηm​∑j=1hlog⁡(det(K~mj​(π)+βm​Id)).\Lambda^{h}_{m}(\pi):=\frac{1}{\eta_{m}}\sum_{j=1}^{h}\log\left(\det(\widetilde{K}^{j}_{m}(\pi)+\beta_{m}I_{d})\right).

The addition of the βm​Id\beta_{m}I_{d} term ensures that the matrix is positive definite and invertible, guaranteeing a well-defined log-determinant. Beyond the trusted occupancy measure weighting, we highlight a key characteristic of our log-determinant regularization. By definition, Λmh\Lambda^{h}_{m} consists of the sum of hh log-determinant terms: log⁡(det(K~mj+βm​Id))\log(\det(\widetilde{K}^{j}_{m}+\beta_{m}I_{d})) for j=1,…,hj=1,\dots,h. Intuitively, this implies that rather than exploring the hh-th layer in isolation, the algorithm requires adequate joint exploration across the first hh layers. This marks another significant algorithmic departure from Algorithm 1 used for tabular MDPs.

Therefore, in the hh-th segment of epoch mm, the policy that the learner applies is

π^mh:=argmaxπ∈ΠR​N​S{V^m−11​(π)+1ηm​Λmh​(π)}.\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m}:=\mathop{\mathrm{argmax}}_{\pi\in\Pi_{RNS}}\left\{\widehat{V}^{1}_{m-1}(\pi)+\frac{1}{\eta_{m}}\Lambda_{m}^{h}(\pi)\right\}.

We provide an intuitive interpretation of this policy. It maximizes a weighted objective that balances exploration and exploitation. Specifically, the first term in the objective, V^m1​(π)\widehat{V}_{m}^{1}(\pi), captures exploitation, since maximizing this value function amounts to maximizing the total expected reward along the trajectory. In contrast, the log-determinant term of the occupancy-weighted feature matrix encourages exploration (Foster et al., 2020): maximizing this quantity is closely related to maximizing the entropy (Zhang et al., 2021), thereby promoting broader exploration of the environment (Dai et al., 2023b). Therefore, by tuning the weight parameter ηm\eta_{m}, the policy achieves a suitable exploration-exploitation trade-off and thus controls the overall regret.

As a notational convenience, under any policy π\pi, we denote the feature covariance matrices weighted by the true observable occupancy measure, ∫s,aϕj​(s,a)​ϕj​(s,a)T​dmj​(s,a,π)\int_{s,a}\phi_{j}(s,a)\phi_{j}(s,a)^{T}d^{j}_{m}(s,a;\pi), and by the estimated occupancy measure, ∫s,aϕj​(s,a)​ϕj​(s,a)T​d^mj​(s,a,π)\int_{s,a}\phi_{j}(s,a)\phi_{j}(s,a)^{T}\widehat{d}^{j}_{m}(s,a;\pi), as Kmj​(π)K^{j}_{m}(\pi) and K^mj​(π)\widehat{K}^{j}_{m}(\pi), respectively.

8 Theoretical Guarantees: Linear MDPs

In this section, we provide our theoretical guarantees. Specifically, we will first present the theoretical guarantees and key lemmas that we obtain per epoch in Subsection 8.1. Later on, in Subsection 8.2, we formally present the theorem regarding the final regret bound. To make the content compact, we will focus on the case where the model class ℳ\mathcal{M} is finite.

8.1 Per-Epoch Theoretical Analysis

In this subsection, we will provide a sequence of lemmas regarding any fixed epoch mm. These lemmas play a similar role compared with those lemmas in Subsection 5.1. The proofs of these lemmas are deferred to Appendix D.

We first show that the executed policy π^mh\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m} enjoys trace control uniformly over all the other policies in ΠR​N​S\Pi_{RNS}, which is very important and parallels Lemma 4 in Section 5.

Lemma 15.

For any m,h,πm,h,\pi, we have that

∑j=1hTr((K~mj​(π^mh)+βm​Id)−1​K~mj​(π))≤\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{h}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}((\widetilde{K}^{j}_{m}(\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m})+\beta_{m}I_{d})^{-1}\widetilde{K}^{j}_{m}(\pi))\leq h​d+ηm​(reg^m−1​(π)−reg^m−1​(π^mh))\displaystyle hd+\eta_{m}(\widehat{\mathrm{reg}}_{m-1}(\pi)-\widehat{\mathrm{reg}}_{m-1}(\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m}))
≤\displaystyle\leq h​d+ηm​reg^m−1​(π).\displaystyle hd+\eta_{m}\widehat{\mathrm{reg}}_{m-1}(\pi).

Intuitively, in a linear MDP, a good exploration policy π\pi should attempt to “maximize” the feature covariance matrix K^mh​(π)\widehat{K}_{m}^{h}(\pi) of the estimated model in the Loewner order, as pointed out in Foster et al. (2020). For any two positive semi-definite matrices AA and BB, if tr⁡(A−1​B)≤c\operatorname{tr}(A^{-1}B)\leq c, then, roughly speaking, one might expect that B⪯c​AB\preceq cA in the Loewner order. Therefore, if we can show that d~mh\widetilde{d}_{m}^{h} is sufficiently close to d^mh\widehat{d}_{m}^{h} in an appropriate sense, then the trace control Lemma 15 may imply that π^mh\widehat{\pi}_{m}^{h} provides effective aggregate exploration over the first hh steps of the unknown underlying model M∗M_{*}.

Thus, our next goal is to show that the trusted occupancy measure closely approximates the estimated occupancy measure d^mh\widehat{d}_{m}^{h}. In tabular MDPs, Lemma 5 provides a pointwise guarantee for every state-action pair between d^mh\widehat{d}_{m}^{h} and d~mh\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}. However, such fine-grained guarantees do not extend to linear MDPs, where the state space 𝒮{\mathcal{S}} is infinite and the action space 𝒜\mathcal{A} is arbitrary. Consequently, for an arbitrary policy π\pi, we must instead quantify the aggregate discrepancy between the integrated measures ∫s,ad^mh​(s,a,π)\int_{s,a}\widehat{d}_{m}^{h}(s,a;\pi) and ∫s,ad~mh​(s,a,π)\int_{s,a}\widetilde{d}_{m}^{h}(s,a;\pi).

Specifically, we have the following lemma.

Lemma 16.

For all m,h,πm,h,\pi, we have

∫s,ad^mh​(s,a,π)−d~mh​(s,a,π)≤(h​cℳζm1/2+h​βm​cℳ2)​h​d+ηm​reg^m−1​(π).\int_{s,a}\widehat{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi)-\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m}(s,a;\pi)\leq\left(\frac{hc_{\mathcal{M}}}{\zeta_{m}^{1/2}}+h\sqrt{\beta_{m}}c_{\mathcal{M}}^{2}\right)\sqrt{hd+\eta_{m}\widehat{\mathrm{reg}}_{m-1}(\pi)}.

Roughly speaking, Lemma 16 states that the aggregate difference between d~mh\widetilde{d}^{h}_{m} and d^mh\widehat{d}^{h}_{m} is upper bounded by 𝒪⁡(h​d+OPENηm​reg^m−1​(π))ζm1/2)\mathcal{O}(\frac{\sqrt{hd}+\sqrt{\eta_{m}\widehat{\mathrm{reg}}_{m-1}(\pi))}}{\zeta_{m}^{1/2}}).

The next lemma, which acts as an equivalent role as Lemma 6, is key to our per-epoch analysis in Linear MDP. Specifically, it establishes that under the offline regression oracle guarantee, the matrix K~mj​(π^mh)\widetilde{K}^{j}_{m}(\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m}) is upper bounded by Kmj​(π^mh)K^{j}_{m}(\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m}) in the Loewner Order, up to a moderate multiplicative factor.

For any mm and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), suppose we have that

𝔼M∗,π^mh​[‖M^m0​(h)−M∗​(h)‖22]≲ℰℳ2​δ/N2​(τm−τm−1),∀h∈[H].\mathbb{E}^{M_{*},\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m}}[\|\widehat{M}^{0}_{m}(h)-M_{*}(h)\|_{2}^{2}]\lesssim\mathcal{E}^{2\delta/N^{2}}_{\mathcal{M}}(\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1}),\forall h\in[H].

Assuming that the hyperparameter ζm\zeta_{m} satisfies that

(H2​d+H​ηm)​(ℰℳ2​δ/N2​(τm−τm−1)+2​βm)<1ζm2,(H^{2}d+H\eta_{m})(\mathcal{E}^{2\delta/N^{2}}_{\mathcal{M}}(\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1})+2\beta_{m})<\frac{1}{\zeta_{m}^{2}},

8.2 Regret Analysis

In this section, we provide the main regret guarantee for linear MDPs. Similar to the guarantees for tabular MDPs in Section 5, we first state the main result. Then, we consider the concrete finite model class case.

Theorem 20.

Assume that we have access to an offline least-squares regression oracle with the statistical guarantee ℰℳδ​(n)≤O⁡(n−γ)\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta}(n)\leq O(n^{-\gamma}) for some γ>0\gamma>0. For any confidence level δ\delta and any geometrically increasing epoch schedule {τm}m=1N\left\{\tau_{m}\right\}_{m=1}^{N} satisfying τm−τm−1≥τm−1\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1}\geq\tau_{m-1}, we set the hyperparameters as follows:

βm=[ℰℳδ/2​N2​(τm−τm−1)]2,\beta_{m}=[\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta/2N^{2}}(\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1})]^{2},
ηm=140​(cℳ2+1)​(cℳ2+cℳ+11)​H2​[ℰℳδ/2​N2​(τm−τm−1)]1/5,\eta_{m}=\frac{1}{40(c_{\mathcal{M}}^{2}+1)(c_{\mathcal{M}}^{2}+c_{\mathcal{M}}+11)H^{2}[\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta/2N^{2}}(\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1})]^{1/5}},
ζm=1[4​H2​d​ηm​ℰℳδ/2​N2​(τm−τm−1)]1/2=10​(cℳ2+1)​(cℳ2+cℳ+11)d​ℰℳδ/2​N2​(τm−τm−1)2/5.\zeta_{m}=\frac{1}{\left[4H^{2}d\eta_{m}\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta/2N^{2}}(\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1})\right]^{1/2}}=\frac{\sqrt{10(c_{\mathcal{M}}^{2}+1)(c_{\mathcal{M}}^{2}+c_{\mathcal{M}}+11)}}{\sqrt{d}\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta/2N^{2}}(\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1})^{2/5}}.

Then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, for Algorithm 2, we have

Reg⁡(T)≲log⁡(1βN)​(cℳ2+1)​(cℳ2+cℳ+11)​d3​H5​∑m=1N(τm−τm−1)​[ℰℳδ/2​N2​(τm−τm−1)]1/5.\mathrm{Reg}(T)\lesssim\log(\frac{1}{\beta_{N}})(c_{\mathcal{M}}^{2}+1)(c_{\mathcal{M}}^{2}+c_{\mathcal{M}}+11)d^{3}H^{5}\sum_{m=1}^{N}(\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1})\left[\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta/2N^{2}}(\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1})\right]^{1/5}.

More specifically, when ℳ\mathcal{M} is finite, we know that ℰℳδ​(n)≲log⁡(|ℳ|/δ)n\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta}(n)\lesssim\frac{\log(|\mathcal{M}|/\delta)}{n} from Lemma 24. Therefore, we have the following two corollaries, which state that for finite model classes, our algorithm achieves sublinear regret with oracle efficiency both on the offline regression oracle and the policy optimization oracle.

Corollary 21.

If TT is known, then by choosing the epoch schedule τm=2​(T/H)1−2−m\tau_{m}=2(T/H)^{1-2^{-m}} for m≥1m\geq 1 and using the offline density estimation oracle as the maximum likelihood estimator, Algorithm 2 satisfies that with a probability of at least 1−δ1-\delta

Reg⁡(T)≲log⁡(T)​(cℳ2+1)​(cℳ2+cℳ+11)​d3​H9/2​log⁡(|ℳ|​log⁡log⁡T/δ)​(log⁡log⁡T)​T4/5.\mathrm{Reg}(T)\lesssim\log(T)(c_{\mathcal{M}}^{2}+1)(c_{\mathcal{M}}^{2}+c_{\mathcal{M}}+11)d^{3}H^{9/2}\log(|\mathcal{M}|\log\log T/\delta)(\log\log T)T^{4/5}.
Corollary 22.

If TT is not known, then by choosing the epoch schedule τm=2m\tau_{m}=2^{m} for m≥1m\geq 1 and using the offline density estimation oracle as the maximum likelihood estimator, Algorithm 2 satisfies that for any δ>0\delta>0, with probability of at least 1−δ1-\delta,

Reg⁡(T)≲log⁡(T)​(cℳ2+1)​(cℳ2+cℳ+11)​d3​H9/2​log⁡(|ℳ|​log​T/δ)​T4/5.\mathrm{Reg}(T)\lesssim\log(T)(c_{\mathcal{M}}^{2}+1)(c_{\mathcal{M}}^{2}+c_{\mathcal{M}}+11)d^{3}H^{9/2}\log(|\mathcal{M}|\log T/\delta)T^{4/5}.

With these two corollaries, we show that our algorithm achieves sublinear regret while requiring only low-frequency calls to the offline regression oracle. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first algorithm to achieve such a guarantee for MDP with infinite state and action spaces.

9 Discussion

In this paper, we introduce DOERL, a novel algorithm that attains the optimal regret bound with merely O⁡(H​log⁡log​T)O(H\log\log T) calls to the offline estimation and planning oracles, assuming a known TT. Notably, this represents the first offline oracle-efficient approach whose planning complexity is strictly independent of the size of the state and action spaces. Building upon this, we further extend DOERL to linear MDPs featuring infinite state spaces and arbitrary action spaces. Consequently, we deliver the first offline oracle-efficient regret minimization algorithm capable of handling MDPs beyond the tabular model.

Our theoretical framework suggests several promising directions for future research. First, the regret bound we establish for linear MDPs is suboptimal. A natural open problem is to develop an offline-oracle-efficient algorithm for linear MDPs with infinite state and action spaces that attains the optimal regret rate. Second, our results raise a broader question about the fundamental limits of offline-oracle-efficient learning. Offline-oracle-efficient regret minimization algorithms are now known for tabular and linear MDPs, but it remains unclear whether general sequential decision-making problems can be solved efficiently using only low-frequency calls to offline oracles. Characterizing the fundamental capability gap between offline and online oracles is an important open problem. Finally, implementing our oracle-efficient algorithms in practical settings and rigorously evaluating their empirical performance is another important direction. We leave these questions for future work.

By the definition of value function, for any model MM and any two policies π1,π2\pi_{1},\pi_{2}, we have VM1​(λ​π1+(1−λ​π2))=λ​VM1​(π1)+(1−λ)​VM1​(π2)V_{M}^{1}(\lambda\pi_{1}+(1-\lambda\pi_{2}))=\lambda V_{M}^{1}(\pi_{1})+(1-\lambda)V_{M}^{1}(\pi_{2}). The value function is linear in λ\lambda.

Meanwhile, by Lemma 27, the function log⁡(det(K~mj​(λ​π^mh+(1−λ)​π)+βm​Id))\log(\det(\widetilde{K}^{j}_{m}(\lambda\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m}+(1-\lambda)\pi)+\beta_{m}I_{d})) is concave in λ\lambda. Therefore, L⁡(λ,π^mh,π)L(\lambda;\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m},\pi) is concave in λ\lambda. Since π^mh\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m} is the maximizer of this function, by the first order ooptimality condition, we have that

Rearranging, we have that

∑j=1hTr((K~mj​(π^mh)+βm​Id)−1​K~mj​(π))≤\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{h}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}((\widetilde{K}^{j}_{m}(\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m})+\beta_{m}I_{d})^{-1}\widetilde{K}^{j}_{m}(\pi))\leq ∑j=1hTr((K~mj​(π^mh)+βm​Id)−1​K~mj​(π^mh))\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{h}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}((\widetilde{K}^{j}_{m}(\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m})+\beta_{m}I_{d})^{-1}\widetilde{K}^{j}_{m}(\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m}))
+ηm​(V^m−11​(π^mh)−V^m−11​(π))\displaystyle+\eta_{m}\left(\widehat{V}_{m-1}^{1}(\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m})-\widehat{V}_{m-1}^{1}(\pi)\right)
≤\displaystyle\leq h​d+ηm​(reg^m−1​(π)−reg^m−1​(π^mh)).\displaystyle hd+\eta_{m}(\widehat{\mathrm{reg}}_{m-1}(\pi)-\widehat{\mathrm{reg}}_{m-1}(\widehat{\pi}^{h}_{m})).

In the last inequality, we use that when A≻BA\succ B, Tr(A−1​B)≤Tr(B−1​B)=d\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}(A^{-1}B)\leq\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}(B^{-1}B)=d.

Thus, we finish the proof. ∎

First, by applying the offline regression oracle guarantee, we have that with probability 1−δ/N1-\delta/N, we have

Then, with probability at least 1−δ/N1-\delta/N, the condition of Lemma 17 is satisfied.

By the first equation in the local simulation lemma (Lemma 29), we have that

+∑h=1H𝔼M^mo​u​t,π[𝔼rh∼RM∗h​(sh,ah)[rh]−𝔼rh∼RM^mo​u​th​(sh,ah)[rh]].\displaystyle+\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}^{\widehat{M}_{m}^{out},\pi}\left[\mathbb{E}_{r_{h}\sim R_{M_{*}}^{h}(s_{h},a_{h})}[r_{h}]-\mathbb{E}_{r_{h}\sim R_{\widehat{M}_{m}^{out}}^{h}(s_{h},a_{h})}[r_{h}]\right].

We consider these two terms separately.

For the term ∑h=1H𝔼M^mo​u​t,π​[[(P∗h−P^mh)​V∗h+1]​(sh+1,π)]\sum_{h=1}^{H}\mathbb{E}^{\widehat{M}_{m}^{out},\pi}\left[\bigl[(P_{*}^{h}-\widehat{P}^{h}_{m})V^{h+1}_{*}\bigr](s_{h+1};\pi)\right], by the definition of the estimated occupancy measure d^mh\widehat{d}^{h}_{m}, we have

≲log⁡(1βN)​(cℳ2+1)​(cℳ2+cℳ+11)​d3​H5​∑m=1N(τm−τm−1)​[ℰℳδ/2​N2​(τm−τm−1)]1/5.\displaystyle\lesssim\log(\frac{1}{\beta_{N}})(c_{\mathcal{M}}^{2}+1)(c_{\mathcal{M}}^{2}+c_{\mathcal{M}}+11)d^{3}H^{5}\sum_{m=1}^{N}(\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1})\left[\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{M}}^{\delta/2N^{2}}(\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1})\right]^{1/5}.

We finish the proof. ∎
